**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on surah 66, verse 1 (part 1 of 2):**

The Surah of *At-Tahrim* is Medinan by the consensus of the scholars, and it has twelve verses. It is also called the Surah of "the Prophet" (*al-Nabi*).

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O Prophet, why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you, seeking the pleasure of your wives? Allah is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful.﴾ (1)

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿O Prophet, why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾ There are five issues (*masa'il*) in this.

**The first issue:** Allah's words, "O Prophet, why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you?" It is established in *Sahih Muslim* from ʿAisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Prophet ﷺ used to stay with Zaynab bint Jahsh and drink honey there. She said: Hafsa and I agreed that whichever of us the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered upon first, she would say, "I smell *maghafir* from you! Have you eaten *maghafir*?" [[The author, may Allah have mercy on him, will explain the meaning of this word and the words that follow in this hadith.]] He entered upon one of them and she said that to him. He said: "Rather, I drank honey at the house of Zaynab bint Jahsh, and I will not return to it." Then it was revealed: ﴿Why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾ up to His words ﴿If you two turn in repentance…﴾ (addressed to ʿAisha and Hafsa), and ﴿When the Prophet confided a matter to one of his wives…﴾ [al-Tahrim: 3], referring to his saying, "Rather, I drank honey."

And also from her: she said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ loved sweets and honey. When he had prayed the ʿAsr prayer, he would go round to his wives and draw near to them. He entered upon Hafsa and stayed with her longer than he usually did. I asked about this, and it was said to me: A woman of her people had given her a jar of honey as a gift, and she gave the Messenger of Allah ﷺ a drink of it. I said: "By Allah, we will certainly devise a plan against him." I mentioned that to Sawda and said: "When he enters upon you, he will draw near to you, so say to him: 'O Messenger of Allah, have you eaten *maghafir*?' He will say to you, 'No.' Then say to him: 'What is this smell?'" (The Messenger of Allah ﷺ disliked that a bad smell be found on him.) "He will say to you: 'Hafsa gave me a drink of honey.' Then say to him: 'Its bees have grazed on *al-ʿurfut*.' I will say that to him too, and you say it, O Safiyya." When he entered upon Sawda, she said: Sawda said, "By Allah, besides whom there is no god, I almost began to speak to him with what you told me, and he was at the door, out of fear of you." When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ drew near, she said: "O Messenger of Allah, have you eaten *maghafir*?" He said: "No." She said: "Then what is this smell?" He said: "Hafsa gave me a drink of honey." She said: "Its bees have grazed on *al-ʿurfut*." When he entered upon me, I said to him the same. Then he entered upon Safiyya and she said the same. When he entered upon Hafsa, she said: "O Messenger of Allah, shall I not give you a drink of it?" He said: "I have no need for it." She said: Sawda said, "Glory be to Allah! By Allah, we have deprived him of it." [[That is, we have prevented him from a drink of honey.]] She said: I said to her, "Be quiet."

So in this narration, the one at whose house he drank the honey was Hafsa, while in the first narration it was Zaynab. Ibn Abi Mulaykah reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he drank it at Sawda's house. It has also been said that it was Umm Salama; this was related by Asbat from al-Suddi, and ʿAta' ibn Abi Muslim said it too. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: "All of this is ignorance, or imagining without knowledge." The rest of his wives said, out of envy and jealousy toward the one at whose house he had drunk it: "We find a smell of *al-maghafir* from you."

*Al-maghafir* is a herb or a gum that has a changed smell, with some sweetness in it. Its singular is *maghfur*. *Jarasat* means "she ate." *Al-ʿurfut* is a plant that has a smell like the smell of wine. The Prophet, peace be upon him, liked to be found with a good fragrance or to smell one, and he disliked a foul smell, because of his private conversation with the angel. This is one opinion.

Another opinion is that he meant by this the woman who had offered herself to the Prophet ﷺ, and he did not accept her for the sake of his wives. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿIkrima. The woman was Umm Sharik.

A third opinion is that the one he forbade was Maria the Copt, whom al-Muqawqis, the ruler of Alexandria, had given him as a gift. Ibn Ishaq said: She was from the district of Anṣanā, [[Anṣanā (with a fatha, then a sukun, a kasra on the unmarked ṣād and the nūn, and a shortened vowel): a town in the regions of Upper Egypt on the eastern side of the Nile.]] from a land called Ḥafn, and he had intercourse with her in Ḥafsa's house. Al-Daraqutni related from Ibn ʿAbbas, from ʿUmar, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered Hafsa's house with his slave-concubine Maria. Hafsa found him with her, for Hafsa had gone out to her father's house. She said to him: "You bring her into my house! You have done this to me among your wives only to humiliate me in your sight." He said to her: "Do not mention this to ʿAisha; she is forbidden to me if I approach her." Hafsa said: "How can she be forbidden to you when she is your slave-girl?" So he swore to her that he would not approach her. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not mention it to anyone." But she mentioned it to ʿAisha, so he took an oath not to enter upon his wives for a month, and he withdrew from them for twenty-nine nights. Then Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: ﴿Why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾, the verse.

**The second issue:** The most sound of these opinions is the first. The weakest is the middle one. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: "As for its weakness in terms of chain, it is because its narrators are not of established integrity ('adala). As for its weakness in meaning, the Prophet ﷺ returning the woman who was given to him is not a prohibition of her, for whoever returns what was given to him does not thereby become forbidden to him. The true meaning of prohibition is after permission. As for the one who narrated that he forbade Maria the Copt, it is better in chain and closer in meaning, but it was not recorded in the *Sahih*, and it was transmitted as a *mursal* (a report with a missing link). Ibn Wahb related from Malik, from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade Umm Ibrahim, and said: 'You are forbidden to me, by Allah, I will certainly not come to you.' So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed about that: ﴿O Prophet, why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾." Ibn al-Qasim related the same from him. Ashhab related from Malik who said: A woman of the Ansar argued with ʿUmar about something, and he was disturbed by that and said: "Women were not like this!" She said: "Yes, indeed, and the wives of the Prophet ﷺ used to argue with him." So he took his garment and went out to Hafsa and said to her: "Do you argue with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ?" She said: "Yes, and if I knew that you disliked what I did, I would not do it." When ʿUmar heard that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had abandoned his wives, he said: "May the nose of Hafsa be rubbed in the dust."

The sound report is that it was about the honey, and that he drank it at Zaynab's house, and ʿAisha and Hafsa supported one another against him in this, so what happened, happened. He swore not to drink it again and kept this secret. The verse was revealed concerning them all.

**The third issue:** Allah's words, ﴿Why do you forbid…﴾. If the Prophet ﷺ forbade something without swearing an oath, then this is not an oath according to us. The saying of a man, "This is forbidden to me" (*hadha ʿalayya haram*), does not make anything forbidden except a wife. Abu Hanifa said: If it is said without qualification, it is taken to refer to food and drink, not clothing, and it is an oath that requires expiation (*kaffara*). Zufar said: It is an oath concerning everything, even movement and existence. The opponent relied on the fact that the Prophet ﷺ forbade honey, and so expiation became binding on him. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths﴾ [al-Tahrim: 2], so He called it an oath. Our evidence is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿O you who believe, do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 87], [[See vol. 6, p. 260.]] and His saying: ﴿Say: Have you considered what Allah has sent down to you of provision, and you have made of it what is forbidden and what is lawful? Say: Has Allah permitted you, or do you fabricate against Allah?﴾ [Yunus: 59]. [[See vol. 8, p. 354.]] So Allah censured the one who forbids what is lawful, and did not make expiation binding on him.

Al-Zajjaj said: No one has the right to forbid what Allah has made lawful, and He did not grant His Prophet ﷺ the right to forbid except what Allah had forbidden to him. So whoever says to his wife or his slave-girl, "You are forbidden to me," without intending divorce or *zihar* (the pre-Islamic pronouncement of a wife as one's mother), this wording requires the expiation of an oath. If he addresses a group of wives and slave-girls with this wording, he owes one expiation. If he forbids food or something else to himself, expiation is not binding on him according to al-Shafiʿi and Malik. Expiation is binding according to Ibn Masʿud, al-Thawri and Abu Hanifa.

**The fourth issue:** The scholars differed concerning a man who says to his wife, "You are forbidden to me," in eighteen opinions:

The first: there is nothing upon him. This was said by al-Shaʿbi, Masruq, Rabiʿa, Abu Salama and Asbagh. In their view, it is like forbidding water and food. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿O you who believe, do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 87], and a wife is among the good things and among what Allah has made lawful. He also said: ﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues describe falsely, "This is lawful and this is forbidden"﴾ [al-Nahl: 116]. Whatever Allah has not forbidden, no one has the right to forbid, nor to make it forbidden by his prohibition. It is not established from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he said of what Allah had made lawful, "It is forbidden to me." He only refrained from Maria because of an oath he had previously made, which was his saying, "By Allah, I will not approach her after today." So it was said to him: "Why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you?", that is, why do you refrain from it because of an oath? That is, proceed with it and make expiation.

The second: it is an oath for which one makes expiation. This was said by Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAisha, may Allah be pleased with them all, and al-Awzaʿi, and it is what the verse implies. Saʿid ibn Jubayr related from Ibn ʿAbbas: "If a man forbids his wife to himself, it is only an oath for which he makes expiation." Ibn ʿAbbas also said: ﴿There is for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent pattern﴾ [al-Ahzab: 21], meaning that the Prophet ﷺ had forbidden his slave-girl, and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you…﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths﴾ [al-Tahrim: 2], so he made expiation for his oath and made the forbidding an oath. Al-Daraqutni recorded this.

The third: expiation is due for it, but it is not an oath. This was said by Ibn Masʿud and also by Ibn ʿAbbas in one of his two reports, and by al-Shafiʿi in one of his two opinions. But there is scrutiny in this view, and the verse rejects it, as will come.

The fourth: it is *zihar*, so the expiation of *zihar* applies to it. This was said by ʿUthman, Ahmad ibn Hanbal and Ishaq.

The fifth: if he intends *zihar* while meaning that she is forbidden like the back of his mother, it is *zihar*. If he intends forbidding her person to himself without divorce, as an absolute prohibition, then the expiation of an oath is due. If he intends nothing, then the expiation of an oath is due upon him. This was said by al-Shafiʿi.

The sixth: it is a revocable divorce (*talaqa raj'iyya*). This was said by ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, al-Zuhri, ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn Abi Salama and Ibn al-Majishun.

The seventh: it is an irrevocable divorce (*talaqa ba'inah*). This was said by Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman and Zayd ibn Thabit. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad related it from Malik.

The eighth: it is three divorces. This was said by ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, Zayd ibn Thabit also, and Abu Hurayra.

The ninth: for a wife who has been consummated it is three, and he is believed concerning one who has not been consummated. This was said by al-Hasan, ʿAli ibn Zayd and al-Hakam. It is also the well-known position of the school of Malik.

The tenth: it is three in every case, and his intention is not accepted in any situation, even if he has not consummated the marriage. [[The phrase "even if he has not consummated" is not in Ibn al-ʿArabi. The wording of Abu Hayyan's *al-Bahr* (vol. 8, p. 289) is: "It is three in both cases, and one is not believed concerning anything." He also attributed it to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn al-Majishun and Ibn Abi Layla.]] This was said by ʿAbd al-Malik in *al-Mabsut*, and Ibn Abi Layla also said so.

Eleventh: it concerns the wife he had not consummated with, one pronouncement; and the one he had consummated with, three. This is the view of Abu Mus'ab and Muhammad ibn Abd al-Hakam. [In another manuscript: "Muhammad ibn al-Hakam."]

Twelfth: if he intended divorce or zihar (the pre-Islamic formula of likening one's wife to one's mother, a form of divorce-like oath), then what he intended applies. If he intended divorce, it is one irrevocable (ba'in) divorce, unless he intended three. If he intended two, it is one. If he intended nothing, it is an oath (yamin), and the man is a mu'li (one who has sworn to abstain from his wife). This is the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions. Zufar said the same, except that he said: if he intended two, we hold him to two.

Thirteenth: his intention regarding zihar carries no weight, and it is only a divorce. This is the view of Ibn al-Qasim.

Fourteenth: Yahya ibn Umar said: it is a divorce. If he takes her back, it is not permissible for him to have intercourse with her until he pays the expiation of zihar.

Fifteenth: if he intended divorce, then whatever number of divorces he intended. If he intended one, it is a revocable (raj'i) divorce. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him. The same was narrated from Abu Bakr, Umar, and others among the Companions and the Successors.

Sixteenth: if he intended three, then three; if one, then one. If he intended an oath, then it is an oath. If he intended nothing, then nothing is incumbent upon him. This is the view of Sufyan. The same was said by al-Awza'i and Abu Thawr, except that they said: if he intended nothing, then it is one.

Seventeenth: his intention is taken into account, and it is not less than one. This was said by Ibn Shihab. If he intended nothing, there is nothing. This was said by Ibn al-'Arabi.

I have seen attributed to Sa'id ibn Jubayr the eighteenth view: that he must free a slave, even if he did not make it zihar. I do not know a basis for it, and it is not far-fetched among the views in my opinion. I say: al-Daraqutni has mentioned it in his Sunan from Ibn Abbas, saying: Al-Husayn ibn Isma'il narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Mansur narrated to us, saying: Rawh narrated to us, saying: Sufyan al-Thawri narrated to us, from Salim al-Aftas, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, that a man came to him and said: "I have made my wife unlawful to me." He said: "You have lied! She is not unlawful to you." Then he recited: "O Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you?" [66:1] "The most severe of expiations is freeing a slave." Some scholars of tafsir said: when this verse was revealed, he expiated for his oath by freeing a slave, and returned to Maria (may Allah bless him and grant him peace). This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam and others.

Fifth: Our scholars said: the cause of disagreement in this matter is that neither in the Book of Allah nor in the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is there a clear text or a sound apparent ruling on which to rely in this question, so scholars pulled it in different directions. Whoever held to the original presumption of non-liability said: there is no ruling, so nothing is binding. As for whoever said it is an oath, he said: Allah named it an oath. As for whoever said that an expiation is obligatory for it and it is not an oath, he based this on one of two matters: first, he thought that Allah the Exalted made expiation obligatory for it even though it was not an oath; second, that the meaning of oath to him is prohibition, so the expiation fell upon the meaning. As for whoever said it is a revocable single divorce, he took the wording in its least sense, and a revocable divorcee is prohibited for intercourse in that way, so the wording is taken to mean that. This applies to Malik, given his statement that a revocably divorced woman is prohibited for intercourse. Similarly is the position of whoever said it is three: he took it in its greatest sense, which is the triple divorce. As for whoever said it is zihar, it is because it is the lowest degree of prohibition, being a prohibition that does not dissolve the marriage. As for whoever said it is an irrevocable single divorce, he relied on the fact that a revocable divorce does not prohibit the divorced woman, whereas an irrevocable divorce does. As for the statement of Yahya ibn Umar, he was cautious by making it a divorce, and when he took her back, he was cautious by making expiation obligatory upon him. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "This is not sound, because it combines two opposites: zihar and divorce cannot both apply to a single wording, so there is no basis for caution in what cannot be validly combined according to the evidence." As for whoever said that it is to be determined by intention regarding the one not yet consummated, it is because one pronouncement makes her irrevocably separated and prohibited by consensus. Likewise, whoever did not hold intention to be decisive said: one pronouncement suffices before consummation in terms of prohibition by consensus, so it suffices, taking the least that is agreed upon. As for whoever said it is three in both cases, it is because he took the greater ruling, for if he had explicitly stated three, they would have taken effect with the one not consummated just as they would with the one consummated, and the meaning must necessarily be the same, namely prohibition." And Allah knows best. All of this concerns a wife. As for a slave-woman, nothing of this applies to her, except that according to Malik, if he intends emancipation by it. The majority of scholars held that he owes an expiation of oath. Ibn al-'Arabi said: the sound view is that it is one single divorce, because if he mentioned divorce, its minimum would be one, unless he multiplies it. Similarly, if he mentions prohibition, its minimum applies, unless he specifies more, such as saying "you are unlawful to me except after another husband," for this explicitly states the intended meaning.

I say: most exegetes hold that the verse was revealed concerning Hafsa, when the Prophet (ﷺ) was alone in her house with his slave-girl; this was mentioned by al-Tha'labi. On this basis, it is as if He said: "What you have prohibited on yourself does not become unlawful for you, but you owe an expiation for an oath," although it also concerns prohibiting honey and the slave-girl. So it is as if He said: "What you prohibited has not become unlawful for you, but you added an oath to the prohibition, so expiate for the oath." This is sound, for the Prophet (ﷺ) prohibited and then swore, as al-Daraqutni mentioned. Al-Bukhari mentioned its meaning in the story of the honey, from Ubayd ibn Umayr, from Aisha, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to drink honey at the house of Zaynab bint Jahsh and would stay with her. So I and Hafsa agreed that whichever of us he entered upon, she should say: "Have you eaten maghafir? I smell maghafir on you!" He said: "No, but I drank honey, and I will not return to it, and I have sworn; do not tell anyone of this," seeking the pleasure of his wives. So by his words "and I will not return to it" he meant in the sense of prohibition, and by "I have sworn" he meant by Allah, as evidence that Allah the Exalted then revealed His reproach to him over that, and referred him to the expiation of oath by His saying: "O Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you" meaning the honey, which he had prohibited by saying "I will not return to it." "Seeking the pleasure of your wives," that is, doing so in pursuit of their satisfaction. "And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful": Forgiving for what made the reproach necessary, Merciful in lifting the blame. It has been said that this was a minor sin. The correct view is that it was a reproach for leaving the better course, and that he never committed any minor or major sin.

There are three issues in this verse.

The first concerns God's words: ﴿God has already ordained for you the dissolving of your oaths﴾. The dissolving (tahlil) of an oath is its expiation (kaffarah), that is, if you wish to make lawful for yourselves what you swore to forgo. This is His words in Surat al-Ma'ida: ﴿its expiation is the feeding of ten needy persons﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 89] (see vol. 6, p. 264). From this it follows that whoever forbids himself some food or drink, it is not made forbidden for him according to us, because the expiation is for the oath, not for the prohibition, as we have explained. Abu Hanifa regards it as an oath in every case, and takes into account the intended benefit in what one forbids. So if one forbids food, he has sworn not to eat it; if a slave-woman, then not to have intercourse with her; if a wife, then it is an ila' (oath of abstention) from her if he has no intention; if he intends zihar, then it is zihar; if he intends divorce, then it is an irrevocable divorce (talaq ba'in). Likewise if he intends two or three (divorces). If he says, "I intended a lie," he is believed between himself and God Most High, but he is not believed in judgment to nullify the ila'. If he says, "Everything lawful upon me is unlawful," then it applies to food and drink if he had no intention; otherwise it applies to what he intended. Al-Shafi'i does not regard it as an oath, but as a cause of expiation concerning women alone [an addition from al-Kashshaf, required by the context]. If he intends divorce, it is revocable according to him, as explained earlier. If he swears not to eat it, he breaks the oath and atones by expiation.

The second issue: if he forbids his slave-woman or his wife, then there is an expiation of oath, as in Sahih Muslim from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "If a man forbids his wife to himself, it is an oath which he must expiate." And he said: ﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of God you have an excellent example﴾.

The third issue: it is said that the Prophet ﷺ made expiation for his oath. But al-Hasan said: he did not make expiation, because the Prophet ﷺ had been forgiven what was past of his sin and what was to come, and the expiation of oaths in this surah was only ordered for the community. The first view is more sound, and that what is meant by this is the Prophet ﷺ.

Then the community follows him in this. We have previously mentioned from Zayd ibn Aslam that he ﷺ made expiation by freeing a slave. And from Muqatil that the Messenger of God ﷺ freed a slave for forbidding Mariyah. And God knows best.

It is also said: that is, God has ordained for you the dissolving of the bond of right-hand possession (milk al-yamin); His words make this clear: ﴿There is no fault in the Prophet concerning what God has ordained for him﴾ [al-Ahzab: 38] (see vol. 14, p. 195), that is, concerning what He prescribed for him regarding the women made lawful to him; that is, He made lawful for you the possession of right hands. So why do you forbid Mariyah to yourself, when God has made her lawful for you?

It is also said: the dissolving of the oath is the exception (istithna'), that is, God has ordained for you the exception that removes one from the oath. Then, according to some, it is permissible to make an exception from oaths whenever one wishes, even after a period has passed. According to the majority, it is not permissible except when joined immediately, so it is as if He said: make an exception after this in what you swear about.

The dissolving (tahlil) of an oath is its dissolution through expiation. The original form is tahlilah, which was assimilated (udghimat). Tafillah is a verbal noun of fa''ala, like tasmiyah and tawsiyah. So tahillah is the dissolving of the oath, as if the oath is a binding and the expiation is a release. It is said: the nahlah is the expiation, that is, it makes lawful for the one who swore what he forbade himself; that is, when he makes expiation, he becomes as one who did not swear.

﴿And God is your Mawla﴾: your Guardian and Helper, by removing the prohibition in what you forbid yourselves, by permitting you to dissolve your oaths through expiation, and by the reward for what you give in expiation.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 66, verse 3:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when the Prophet confided to one of his wives a statement﴾. That is: and remember when the Prophet confided to Hafsah a statement, meaning the prohibition of Mariyah upon himself, and his instruction to her to keep that secret. Al-Kalbi said: he confided to her that your father and the father of Aishah would be his successors over my community after me, and Ibn Abbas said the same. He said: he confided to her the matter of the caliphate after him, and Hafsah disclosed it. Al-Daraqutni related in his Sunan, from al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when the Prophet confided to one of his wives a statement﴾, that he said: Hafsah came upon the Prophet ﷺ together with Umm Ibrahim, and he said: (Do not inform Aishah), and he said to her: (Indeed your father and her father will rule, or will take charge, after me, so do not inform Aishah). He said: Hafsah went and informed Aishah, so Allah made him aware of it, and he acknowledged part of it and turned away from part of it. He said: he turned away from his saying: (Indeed your father and her father will be after me). The Messenger of Allah ﷺ disliked that this be spread among the people.

﴿So when she informed of it﴾: that is, she told Aishah of it, because of a friendship that existed between them, and the two of them were allies against the wives of the Prophet ﷺ.

﴿And Allah made him aware of it﴾: that is, Allah informed him that she had disclosed it. Talhah ibn Musarrif read ﴿fa-lamma anba'at﴾, and both are dialects: anba'a and naba'a. The meaning of ﴿he acknowledged part of it and turned away from part of it﴾ is: he made Hafsah aware of some of what had been revealed to him, that she had informed Aishah of what he had forbidden her to tell her, and he turned away from part of it out of generosity, as said by al-Suddi. Al-Hasan said: no noble person ever scrutinizes to the end; Allah the Exalted said: he acknowledged part of it and turned away from part of it. Muqatil said: that is, he informed her of some of what she had said to Aishah, which was the matter of his concubine, and he did not inform her of part, which was Hafsah's saying to Aishah: indeed Abu Bakr and Umar will rule after him. The common reading is ﴿'arrafa﴾ with shaddah, and its meaning is what we have mentioned. Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred it, and the evidence for it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and turned away from part of it﴾, meaning he did not make her aware of it. Had it been without shaddah, He would have said in its opposite: and denied part of it. Ali, Talhah ibn Musarrif, Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Kalbi, al-Kisa'i and al-A'mash, from Abu Bakr, read ﴿'arafa﴾ without shaddah. Ata said: whenever a man read to Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami ﴿'arrafa﴾ with shaddah, he would pelt him with stones. Al-Farra' said: the interpretation of His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿'arafa ba'dahu﴾ with the lighter form means: he was angry about it and requited it, and it is like your saying to one who has wronged you: "I will certainly make you know what you did," that is, I will repay you for it. The Prophet ﷺ requited her by divorcing her with a single divorce. Umar said: had there been any good in the family of al-Khattab, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would not have divorced you. Then Jibril commanded him to take her back, and he interceded on her behalf. The Prophet ﷺ withdrew from his wives for a month, and he sat in the upper chamber of Mariyah, mother of Ibrahim, until the verse of prohibition was revealed, as previously mentioned. It is also said: he intended to divorce her until Jibril said to him: "Do not divorce her, for she is fasting often, standing in prayer often, and she is among your wives in Paradise," so he did not divorce her.

﴿So when he informed her of it﴾: that is, the Prophet informed Hafsah of what Allah had made him aware of.

﴿She said: "Who informed you of this?"﴾, O Messenger of Allah, concerning me. She thought that Aishah had told him. He, peace be upon him, said: (The All-Knowing, the All-Aware informed me), that is, He to whom nothing is hidden. This took the place of the two objects of anba'a. The first naba'a transitively takes one object, and the second naba'a takes one object, because naba'a and anba'a, when they do not govern a subject and predicate, may be used with one object or with two; but when they govern a subject and predicate, each of them takes three objects. Limiting them to two without the third is not permitted, because the third is in origin the predicate of the subject, so it is not omitted, just as the subject is not omitted without the predicate.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 66, verse 4:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If you two turn in repentance to Allah﴾. He means Hafsah and Aisha. He urged them to repent for what had come from them of inclining toward what opposed the love of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

(﴿Then indeed your hearts have inclined﴾). That is, they deviated and swerved from the truth. It means that they loved what the Prophet (ﷺ) disliked, namely avoiding his slave-girl and avoiding honey. The Prophet (peace be upon him) loved honey and women. Ibn Zayd said: "Their hearts inclined in that it pleased them that he should abstain from his umm walad (the mother of his child), so what he disliked pleased them." It was also said: "Your hearts have inclined toward repentance." He said: "Your hearts have inclined" (ṣaghat qulūbuKumā, using the dual form), and did not say "Your two hearts have inclined" (ṣagā qalbākumā). It is the custom of the Arabs, when they mention two things of a pair, to join them in the plural form, because it is not ambiguous. This meaning has already been discussed in Surah al-Ma'idah in His saying: ﴿So cut off their hands﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 38] [[See vol. 6 p. 173]]. It was also said: whenever the dual is combined with an attached pronoun, the plural form is more fitting, because it is easier and lighter. His saying ﴿Then indeed your hearts have inclined﴾ is not the answer (jaza') to the conditional clause, because this inclining had already occurred. So the answer of the conditional is omitted, being understood, meaning: "If you two repent, it would be better for you, since your hearts have inclined."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you cooperate against him﴾. That is, if you two band together and cooperate against the Prophet (ﷺ) with disobedience and harm. In Sahih Muslim, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "I remained for a year wanting to ask Umar ibn al-Khattab about a verse, but I could not ask him out of awe of him. Until he went out on Hajj and I went out with him. When he returned, and we were on part of the road, he turned aside to the arak [[al-Arak: the trees, singular arakah]] for some need of his. I waited until he finished, then I walked with him and said: 'O Commander of the Believers, who are the two wives of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who banded together against him?' He said: 'They are Hafsah and Aisha.' I said to him: 'By Allah, I have wanted to ask you about this for a year, but I could not, out of awe of you.' He said: 'Do not do so. Ask me whatever you think I have knowledge of, and if I know it, I will inform you...'" and he mentioned the hadith.

(﴿Then indeed Allah is his protector﴾). That is, his Guardian and Helper, so that their cooperation against him does not harm him.

(﴿And Gabriel and the righteous among the believers﴾). Ikrimah and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they are Abu Bakr and Umar, because they were the fathers of Aisha and Hafsah, and they had been a support to him against them. It was also said: "the righteous among the believers" is Ali (may Allah be pleased with him). It was also said: the best of the believers. Salih (righteous) here is a noun of genus, like His saying: ﴿By time. Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [al-'Asr: 1-2]. This was said by al-Tabari. It was also said: "the righteous among the believers" are the prophets; this was said by al-'Ala' ibn Ziyadah, Qatadah and Sufyan. Ibn Zayd said: they are the angels. Al-Suddi said: they are the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was also said: "Salih al-mu'minin" is not a singular form; rather it is ṣāliḥū al-mu'minīn (the righteous of the believers), so the righteous are attributed to the believers, and it is written without a waw according to the pronunciation, because the singular and plural forms are the same in it, just as some things in the Mushaf are written in a way that follows the pronunciation rather than the orthography. In Sahih Muslim, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated to me, saying: When the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) withdrew from his wives, I entered the mosque, and the people were tapping the ground with pebbles [[i.e., striking the earth with it, like one who is worried and pensive]] and saying: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has divorced his wives.' That was before they were commanded to veil. Umar said: I said, 'I will surely find out about this today.' So I entered upon Aisha and said: 'Daughter of Abu Bakr, has your affair reached the point that you harm the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?' She said: 'What is it to me and to you, son of al-Khattab! Attend to your storage chest!' [[i.e., attend to the admonishing of your daughter Hafsah. The 'aybah is a container in which a person keeps his finest clothes and precious goods, so she compared his daughter to it.]] So I entered upon Hafsah bint Umar and said to her: 'O Hafsah, has your affair reached the point that you harm the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)? By Allah, you know that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) does not love you, and were it not for me, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would have divorced you.' She wept most bitterly, so I said to her: 'Where is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?' She said: 'He is in his storeroom in the upper chamber (mashrabah).' So I entered, and there was Rabah, the servant of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), sitting on the threshold of the upper chamber, with his legs hanging down over a trunk of wood, which was a notched log by which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would ascend and descend. I called out: 'O Rabah, ask permission for me to enter upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' Rabah looked at the chamber, then looked at me, and said nothing. Then I said: 'O Rabah, ask permission for me to enter upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' Rabah looked at the chamber, then looked at me, and said nothing. Then I raised my voice and said: 'O Rabah, ask permission for me to enter upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for I think the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) thought that I came because of Hafsah. By Allah, if the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commands me to strike her neck, I will surely strike her neck.' I raised my voice, and he gestured to me to come up. So I entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he was lying on a mat. I sat down, and he pulled his waist-wrapper over him, and he had nothing else on. The mat had left its mark on his side. I looked around the storeroom of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and there, I saw a handful of barley, about a sa', and similar to it some tanning leaves in a corner of the chamber, and a hide [[al-Afiq: a hide that has not been fully tanned]] hanging. He said: My eyes welled up with tears. He said: (What makes you weep, son of al-Khattab?) I said: 'O Prophet of Allah, how could I not weep when this mat has left its mark on your side, and this is your storeroom, and I see in it nothing but what I see! Caesar and Chosroes are amid fruits and rivers, while you are the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his chosen one, and this is your storeroom!' He said: (O son of al-Khattab, are you not pleased that for us is the Hereafter and for them is this world?) I said: 'Yes.' He said: I entered upon him when I entered, and I saw anger in his face. So I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what troubles you of the affairs of women? If you have divorced them, then indeed Allah is with you, and His angels, and Gabriel and Michael, and I and Abu Bakr and the believers are with you.' I have rarely spoken, and praise be to Allah, a word except that I hoped Allah, Mighty and Majestic, would confirm the word I was saying [[An addition from Sahih Muslim.]]. Then this verse was revealed, the verse of choice: ﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will substitute for him wives better than you﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5]. And ﴿And if you cooperate against him, then indeed Allah is his protector, and Gabriel, and the righteous of the believers, and the angels after that are supporters﴾. Aisha bint Abi Bakr and Hafsah used to band together against the rest of the wives of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, have you divorced them?' He said: (No.) I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I entered the mosque and the Muslims were tapping the ground with pebbles, saying: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has divorced his wives. Shall I go down and inform them that you have not divorced them?' He said: (Yes, if you wish.) I kept talking to him until the anger left his face, and until he smiled, showing his teeth, and he had one of the most beautiful smiles among people. Then the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) came down, and I came down. I came down clinging to the trunk, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came down as though walking on the ground, not touching it with his hand. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, you were in the chamber for only twenty-nine days.' He said: (The month may be twenty-nine days.) Then I stood at the door of the mosque and called out at the top of my voice: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has not divorced his wives.' And this verse was revealed: ﴿And when a matter of security or fear comes to them, they spread it around. But if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them, those who [can] draw correct conclusions would have known about it from them﴾ [al-Nisa': 83] [[See vol. 5 p. 291]]. So I was the one who drew that conclusion from the matter, and Allah revealed the verse of choice."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and Gabriel﴾. Concerning it there are several dialects, which were discussed in Surah al-Baqarah [[See vol. 2 p. 37]]. It is permissible for it to be coordinated with "his protector," and the meaning would be: Allah is his Protector, and Gabriel is his Protector. In that case, one does not stop at "his protector" but stops at "Gabriel," and "the righteous of the believers" is the subject (mubtada'), with "the angels" coordinated to it, and "supporters" as the predicate (khabar), and it has the meaning of the plural. The "righteous of the believers" is Abu Bakr; this was said by al-Musayyab ibn Sharik. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is Umar. Ikrimah said: Abu Bakr and Umar. Shaqiq narrated from Abdullah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Then indeed Allah is his protector, and Gabriel, and the righteous of the believers﴾, that he said: "The righteous of the believers is Abu Bakr and Umar." It was also said: it is Ali. From Asma' bint Umays, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: (And the righteous of the believers is Ali ibn Abi Talib)." Other views have been mentioned beyond these, which were discussed earlier. It is also permissible that "and Gabriel" be the subject, and what follows it be coordinated to it, with "supporters" as the predicate, also in the sense of the plural. In that case one stops at "his protector." It is also permissible that "Gabriel and the righteous of the believers" be coordinated to "his protector," and one stops at "the believers," and "and the angels after that are supporters" is a new beginning (ibtida') and predicate (khabar). The meaning of ẓahīr is "helpers," and it has the meaning of ẓuhara' (plural), like His saying: ﴿And how excellent those companions are as a company﴾ [al-Nisa': 69] [[See vol. 5 p. 271]]. Abu Ali said: the form fa'il has come for the plural, like His saying: ﴿No intimate friend will ask about his intimate friend, though they will be shown them﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 10-11] [[See p. 284 of this part]]. It was also said: the cooperation between them was in dictating to the Prophet (peace be upon him) concerning expenditure, and for this reason he took an oath (ila') against them for a month and withdrew from them. In Sahih Muslim, from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: "Abu Bakr came asking permission to enter upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he found people sitting at his door, and none of them had been given permission. He said: So Abu Bakr was given permission and entered. Then Umar came and asked permission, and he was given permission. He found the Prophet (ﷺ) sitting around him with his wives, silent and downcast. He said: So Umar said: 'I will surely say something that will make the Prophet (ﷺ) laugh.' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if only you had seen the daughter of Kharijah, who asked me for expenditure, so I stood up to her and struck her neck.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) laughed and said: (They are around me as you see, asking me for expenditure.) Abu Bakr got up to Aisha to strike her neck, and Umar got up to Hafsah to strike her neck, both saying: 'You ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for what he does not have!' They said: 'By Allah, we will never ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for anything again that he does not have.' Then he withdrew from them for a month or twenty-nine days. Then this verse was revealed to him: ﴿O Prophet, say to your wives...﴾ until ﴿for the good-doers among you a great reward﴾ [al-Ahzab: 28-29]." This hadith. It has been mentioned in Surah "al-Ahzab" [[See vol. 14 p. 163]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 66, verse 5:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him in exchange wives better than you﴾. It has already been mentioned in the Sahih that this verse was revealed through the tongue of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him [[See p. 191 of this part.]]. Then it was said: every "perhaps" (ʿasā) in the Qur'an is binding, except this one. It was also said: it is binding, but Allah, mighty and majestic, made it conditional upon a condition, which is divorce, and He did not divorce them.

(That He should give him in exchange wives better than you) because if you were better than them, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would not have divorced you. This is the meaning reported from al-Suddi. It was also said: this is a promise from Allah, exalted is He, to His Messenger ﷺ that if he divorced them in this world, He would marry him to wives better than them in this world. It is read as "yubaddilahu" with shaddah and without shaddah. Al-tabdil (substitution) and al-ibdal (replacement) have the same meaning, like al-tanzil and al-inzal. Allah knew that he would not divorce them, but He informed of His power, and that if he divorced them He would replace him with wives better than them, as a warning to them. It is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people other than you﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 258]] [Muhammad: 38]. This is an informing of His power and a warning to them, not that there exists in the world anyone better than the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Muslimat﴾, meaning sincere (mukhlisat), said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr. It was also said: its meaning is those who submit to the command of Allah and the command of His Messenger.

(Mu'minat) affirming what they were commanded and forbidden.

(Qanitat) obedient. Al-qunut is obedience. It has already been mentioned [[See vol. 2, p. 86 and vol. 3, p. 213]].

(Ta'ibat) that is, from their sins, said by al-Suddi. It was also said: returning (to Allah), those who abandon the desires of their own selves.

(ʿAbidat) that is, those who worship Allah, exalted is He, abundantly. Ibn ʿAbbas said: every "worship" (ʿibadah) in the Qur'an means monotheism (tawhid).

(Sa'ihat) fasting (sa'imat), said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan and Ibn Jubayr. Zayd ibn Aslam and his son ʿAbd al-Rahman and Yaman said: emigrants (muhajirat). Zayd said: there is no sightseeing (siyahah) in the community of Muhammad ﷺ except emigration (al-hijrah). Al-siyahah is wandering in the earth. Al-Farra' and al-Qutabi and others said: the fasting person is called a sa'ih because the wanderer carries no provisions, but eats wherever he finds food. It was also said: those who go forth in obedience to Allah, mighty and majestic, from sa'ah al-ma' meaning the water went away. This has already passed in Surat Bara'ah [[See vol. 8, p. 269.]], and all praise is due to Allah.

(Thayyibat wa abkaran) meaning among them are thayyib and among them are bikr. It was also said: the thayyib was called thayyib because she returns to her husband if he remains with her, or to another if he parts from her. It was also said: because she has settled (thabat) in her parents' house. This is more correct, because not every thayyib returns to a husband. As for the bikr, she is the virgin, called bikr because she is in the first state in which she was created. Al-Kalbi said: by the thayyib he meant someone like Asiya, the wife of Pharaoh, and by the bikr someone like Maryam daughter of ʿImran. I say: this only holds according to the view of those who say that the substitution is a promise from Allah to His Prophet that if he divorced them in this world, He would marry him in the Hereafter to wives better than them. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 66, verse 6:

There is one issue here: the command for a person to protect himself and his family from the Fire. Al-Dahhak said: its meaning is "Protect yourselves, and let your family protect themselves from a fire." ʿAli ibn Abi Talha narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: "Protect yourselves, and command your families to remember Allah and to supplicate, until Allah protects them through you." ʿAli (may Allah be pleased with him), Qatada and Mujahid said: "Protect yourselves by your deeds, and protect your families by your instruction." Ibn al-ʿArabi said: this is the correct view, and the jurisprudential point given by the conjunction (al-ʿatf), which requires that the conjoined and the thing conjoined share in the sense of the verb, is as in his saying:

"I fed her chaff and cool water" [A well-known rajaz verse whose speaker is unknown. Its completion is: "until the small-eyed one's eyes were dispersed." See al-Insaf and Sharh al-Shawahid, vol. 6, p. 95.]

And as in his saying:

"And I saw your husband in battle... wearing a sword and a spear"

So a man must reform himself through obedience, and reform his family in the manner of a shepherd tending his flock. In the authentic hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Each of you is a shepherd and each of you is responsible for his flock. The leader over the people is a shepherd and is responsible for them, and a man is a shepherd over his household and is responsible for them." It is in this light that al-Hasan explained this verse by saying: "He commands them and forbids them." Some scholars said: when He said "Protect yourselves," children are included, because the child is a part of him, just as they are included in the Exalted's saying: "Nor upon yourselves that you eat from your houses" [al-Nur: 61]. They were not singled out for mention as other relatives were. So he teaches him what is lawful and unlawful, keeps him away from sins and sinful acts, and other rulings besides these. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The right of a child upon the father is that he give him a good name, teach him writing, and marry him off when he reaches maturity." He (ﷺ) also said: "No father has given his child a better gift than good manners." ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb narrated from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Command your children to pray at seven, strike them for it at ten, and separate them in their beds." This was transmitted by a group of the people of hadith, and this is the wording of Abu Dawud. He also transmitted from Samura ibn Jundab who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Command the child to pray when he reaches seven years, and if he reaches ten years, strike him for it." Likewise, he informs his family of the time of prayer, the obligation of fasting, and the obligation to break the fast when it becomes due, relying in that on the sighting of the crescent. Muslim narrated that when the Prophet (ﷺ) performed the witr prayer, he would say: "Rise and perform witr, O ʿAisha." It is also narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on a man who rises at night, prays, and wakes his wife; if she does not rise, he sprinkles water on her face. May Allah have mercy on a woman who rises at night to pray and wakes her husband; if he does not rise, she sprinkles water on his face." And from this is his saying (ﷺ): "Wake up the companions of the chambers." This falls under the generality of Allah's saying: "And cooperate in righteousness and piety" [al-Ma'idah: 2]. Al-Qushayri mentioned that ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) said when this verse was revealed: "O Messenger of Allah, we protect ourselves, but how do we protect our families?" He said: "You forbid them what Allah has forbidden you, and you command them with what Allah has commanded." Muqatil said: this is a duty upon him regarding himself, his children, his wife, his servants, and his female servants. Al-Kiya said: it is incumbent upon us to teach our children and our families religion and goodness, and such manners as they cannot do without. This is the saying of the Exalted: "And enjoin prayer upon your family and be steadfast in it" [Ta-Ha: 132]. It is like the saying of the Exalted to the Prophet (ﷺ): "And warn your closest kinsmen" [al-Shu'ara': 214]. And in the hadith: "Command them to pray when they are seven years old."

"Its fuel is people and stones" has been discussed earlier in Surat al-Baqarah.

"Over it are angels, harsh and severe": meaning the angels of punishment (al-zabaniya), harsh of heart, who show no mercy when asked for mercy. They were created from anger, and the punishment of creatures was made beloved to them, just as eating and drinking were made beloved to the children of Adam. "Severe" means severe of bodies. It was said: harsh in words and severe in deeds. It was also said: harsh in seizing the people of the Fire and severe against them; one says, "So-and-so is severe upon so-and-so," meaning he is strong against him, punishing him with every kind of punishment. It was also said: by "harsh" is meant the largeness of their bodies, and by "severity" their strength. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the distance between the shoulders of one of them is a journey of a year, and the strength of one of them is that he may be struck with an iron rod and by that single blow push seventy thousand people into the bottom of Hell. Ibn Wahb mentioned, saying: ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd told us, saying: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning the guardians of Hell: "The distance between the shoulders of one of them is like the distance between the east and the west."

His saying, may He be exalted: "They do not disobey Allah in what He commands them," meaning they do not oppose Him in His command, whether by addition or subtraction.

"And they do what they are commanded": meaning at its proper time, so they neither delay it nor advance it. It was said: meaning their pleasure lies in obeying Allah's command, just as the joy of the people of Paradise lies in being in Paradise. This was mentioned by some of the Mu'tazila, who held that it is impossible for obligation to occur tomorrow. The belief of the people of truth is not hidden: that Allah imposes obligation upon the servant today and tomorrow, and obligation is not denied with respect to the angels. And Allah does what He wills.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 66, verse 7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have disbelieved, do not make excuses today﴾, for your excuse will not benefit you. This prohibition is for the confirmation of despair.

(You are only being recompensed for what you used to do) in the world. Its parallel is: ﴿So on that Day, those who did wrong will not benefit from their excuse, nor will they be allowed to make amends﴾ [al-Rum: 57]. And this has already been discussed.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 66, verse 8:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, repent to Allah with sincere repentance﴾. In this there are two issues.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, "O you who have believed, repent to Allah," is a command to repentance (tawbah), and it is an obligation upon every individual (fard 'ala al-a'yan) in all circumstances and at all times. Its explanation and the discussion concerning it have already been presented in "al-Nisa'" and elsewhere [[see vol. 5, p. 90]].

"Sincere repentance" (tawbatan nasuha): The scholars and the people of the hearts have differed in their expressions regarding sincere repentance (tawbah nasuh) into twenty-three sayings. It has been said: it is that after which there is no return, just as milk does not return to the udder. This is narrated from 'Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Mu'adh ibn Jabal, may Allah be pleased with them. Mu'adh traced it back to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Qatadah said: "Nasuh" means truthful and counselling (al-sadiqah al-nasihah). It has also been said: sincere (al-khalisah); it is said "nasaha," meaning he made his speech pure for him.

Al-Hasan said: "Nasuh" is that one hates the sin which one once loved, and seeks forgiveness for it whenever one remembers it.

It has been said: it is that repentance in which one does not trust that it will be accepted, and remains in apprehension regarding it.

It has been said: it is that after which no further repentance is needed.

Al-Kalbi said: sincere repentance is regret in the heart, seeking forgiveness with the tongue, abandoning the sin, and being resolved that one will not return to it.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is accepted repentance, and it is not accepted unless there are three conditions in it: fear that it will not be accepted, hope that it will be accepted, and persistence in acts of obedience.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: it is a repentance by which you counsel your own souls.

Al-Qurazi said: it comprises four things: seeking forgiveness with the tongue, abandoning sin with the body, resolving with the heart never to return, and forsaking evil companions.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: the sign of sincere repentance is four things: few [possessions] (al-qillah), sickness (al-'illah), humility (al-dhillah), and strangeness (al-ghurbah).

Al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad said: it is that the sin be before one's eyes, such that one continues as if looking at it.

Similar to this, from Ibn al-Simak: that you set before your eyes the sin in which you were shameless before Allah, and prepare for what awaits you.

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: it is that the earth becomes constricted for you despite its vastness, and your own self becomes constricted for you, like the three who were left behind [[The three who were left behind are: Ka'b ibn Malik, Murarah ibn al-Rabi' al-'Amri, and Hilal ibn Umayyah al-Waqifi. See vol. 8, p. 282 and vol. 2, p. 907 of Ibn Hisham's Sirah, Oriya Press edition.]].

Abu Bakr al-Wasiti said: it is a repentance not for the loss of a substitute, because whoever sins in this world for the comfort of his self and then repents seeking its comfort in the Hereafter, his repentance is for the preservation of his self, not for Allah.

Abu Bakr al-Daqqaq al-Misri said: sincere repentance is returning wrongs, seeking the pardon of adversaries, and persistence in acts of obedience.

Ruwaym said: it is that you become a face for Allah without a back, just as you were a back for Him at the time of disobedience without a face.

Dhu al-Nun said: the signs of sincere repentance are three: little speech, little food, and little sleep.

Shaqiq said: it is that its possessor greatly blames himself and does not cease from regret, so that he may be saved from its calamities in safety.

Sari al-Saqati said: sincere repentance is not sound except with counsel to oneself and to the believers, for whoever keeps company with his repentance loves that people be like him.

Al-Junayd said: sincere repentance is that one forgets the sin and never mentions it again, for whoever's repentance is sound becomes a lover of Allah, and whoever loves Allah forgets what is other than Allah.

Dhu al-Udhunayn said: it is that its possessor has flowing tears and a heart turning away from sins [[Dhu al-Udhunayn: a title of Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, which the Prophet (ﷺ) gave him. It is said its meaning is encouragement toward good listening and awareness. It is also said that this saying is among his playful remarks, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him.]].

Fath al-Mawsili said: its signs are three: opposing desire, much weeping, and enduring hunger and thirst.

Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah al-Tustari said: it is the repentance of the people of the Sunnah and the community, because the innovator has no repentance, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah has forbidden every possessor of innovation to repent."

From Hudhayfah: it is sufficient for a man of evil that he repents from a sin and then returns to it.

The origin of "sincere repentance" (al-tawbah al-nasuh) is from purity (al-khulus); it is said: "This is pure honey (asal nasih)" when it has been purified of wax. It has also been said: it is derived from al-nasaha, which is sewing (al-khiyatah). As for taking it from this, there are two views: first, because it is a repentance that has firmly secured obedience to Him and bound it, just as the tailor firmly secures and binds the garment with his stitching. Second, because it has joined him with the friends of Allah and attached him to them, just as the tailor joins the garment and attaches one part to another.

The reading of the common people is "nasuhan" with a fatha on the nun, as an adjective of "tawbah," like "imra'atun sabur," meaning a repentance that reaches its utmost in counsel. Al-Hasan, Kharijah and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read it with a damma, and its interpretation according to this reading is: repentance of counsel for your own souls. It has also been said: "nusuh" may be the plural of "nasih," and it may be a verbal noun; it is said "nasaha nasahah wa nusuhan." Verbal nouns of the pattern fa'alah and fu'ul sometimes coincide, such as "al-dhahab" and "al-dhuhub." Al-Mubarrad said: he meant a repentance possessing counsel; it is said "nasahtu nushan wa nasahatan wa nusuhan."

The second issue: concerning the things from which repentance is made and how repentance is made from them. The scholars said: the sin from which repentance is made is not free of being either a right of Allah or a right of the sons of Adam. If it is a right of Allah, such as abandoning a prayer, then repentance from it is not valid until, together with regret, one makes up for what was missed. Likewise if it is abandoning fasting or neglecting zakat. If it is killing a soul without right, then one must submit oneself to retaliation (qisas) if it is due and he is being sought for it. If it is slander (qadhf) that entails the hadd punishment, then he must offer his back for the lashing if he is being sought for it. If he is pardoned, regret and resolve never to return, with sincerity, suffice him. Likewise if he is pardoned in a killing in exchange for property, he must pay it if he is able to, Allah the Exalted says: "But if he is pardoned by his brother, let there be a follow-up with fairness and payment to him with good conduct" [[see vol. 2, p. 253]] [al-Baqarah: 178]. If it is a hadd among the hudud of Allah, whatever it may be, then when he repents to Allah the Exalted with true regret, it falls from him. Allah the Exalted has explicitly stated the dropping of the hadd from the muharibun (highwaymen) if they repent before being overpowered. This is evidence that it does not drop from them if they repent after being overpowered, as explained earlier [[see vol. 6, p. (174)]]. Likewise, drinkers, thieves and fornicators, if they reform and repent and this is known of them, and then they are brought before the ruler, it is not fitting for him to inflict the hadd upon them. But if they are brought to him and say, "We have repented," they are not released, and in this state they are like the muharibun when they have been overpowered. This is the doctrine of al-Shafi'i.

If the sin concerns injustices against people, then repentance from it is not valid except by returning it to its owner and getting out from it, whether it be a specific thing or otherwise, if he is able to do so. If he is not able, then the resolve is to pay it as soon as he is able, at the earliest and swiftest time. If it harmed one of the Muslims and that one does not perceive it or does not know from where it came, then he removes that harm from him, then asks him to pardon him and to seek forgiveness for him; when he pardons him, the sin has fallen from him. If he sends someone to request that on his behalf, and that wronged person pardons his wrongdoer, whether he identifies him or not, that is valid. If a man wrongs another man by frightening him without right, or distressing him, or slapping him, or striking him without right, or beating him with a whip so as to cause him pain, then comes to him seeking pardon, regretful for what he did, resolved never to return, and keeps humbling himself to him until his soul is content and he pardons him, that sin falls from him. Likewise if he disgraced him with insult for which there is no hadd.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It may be that your Lord will remove from you your misdeeds﴾. "'Asa" (it may be) from Allah is binding (wajibah). This is the meaning of his saying, peace be upon him: "The one who repents from sin is like one who has no sin." And "an" (that) is in the position of the subject of "'asa" [[What is between the brackets is from the printed edition, and there is a blank in what remains of the manuscripts.]].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and admit you﴾ is conjoined to "yukaffira." Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "wa yudkhilkum" in the jussive, conjoined to the position of "'asa an yukaffira." As if it were said: "Repent, which will necessitate the expiation of your misdeeds and will admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow."

(The day Allah will not disgrace the Prophet) The governing element of "yawm" is "yudkhilukum" or an implied verb. The meaning of "yukhzi" here is "to punish," i.e., He will not punish him nor those who believed with him.

(Their light runs before them and on their right hands) This was discussed in the surah "al-Hadid" [[see vol. 17, p. 243]].

(They say: Our Lord, perfect for us our light and forgive us; indeed You are over all things Competent) Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others said: this is the supplication of the believers when Allah extinguishes the light of the hypocrites, as explained earlier in the surah "al-Hadid" [[see vol. 17, p. 245]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 66, verse 9:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh with them﴾. In this there is one issue, namely severity in the religion of Allah. So He commanded him to strive against the disbelievers with the sword, with good admonitions, and with the call to Allah; and against the hypocrites with harshness and the establishing of proof. He was also to inform them of their condition in the Hereafter, and that they have no light by which they may pass over the Sirat (the bridge over Hell) along with the believers. Al-Hasan said: that is, strive against them by enforcing the prescribed punishments (hudud) upon them, for they used to commit acts that required the hudud, and the hudud were enforced upon them.

﴿And their refuge is Hell﴾: this refers to both groups.

﴿And wretched is the destination﴾: that is, the place of return.

God struck this example as a warning that no one will avail anyone in the Hereafter, neither a close relative nor a kinsman, when religion separates them. The name of Noah's wife was Wahila, and the name of Lot's wife was Wali'a, as stated by Muqatil. Al-Dahhak reported from A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her): Gabriel descended upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him that the name of Noah's wife was Wa'ila and the name of Lot's wife was Wahila.

(But they betrayed them) Ikrima and al-Dahhak said: by disbelief. Sulayman ibn Ruqayya [in L: "Qutta"; in Tafsir al-Tabari: "Qays"] reported from Ibn Abbas: Noah's wife would tell the people that he was a madman, and Lot's wife would inform on his guests. And from him: the wife of no prophet ever committed adultery. This is a consensus of the exegetes, as mentioned by al-Qushayri. Their betrayal was only in religion, and both of them were polytheists. It was also said: they were hypocrites. And it was said: their betrayal was tale-bearing; when Allah revealed something to them, they would disclose it to the polytheists, as stated by al-Dahhak. It was also said: whenever a guest came to Lot, Lot's wife would light smoke to let her people know that a guest had arrived, because of what they were engaged in of having intercourse with men.

(But they availed them nothing against Allah) That is, Noah and Lot, despite their honour before Allah the Exalted, did not repel anything of Allah's punishment from their two wives when they disobeyed; this is a warning that punishment is averted by obedience, not by kinship. It is said that the disbelievers of Mecca mocked, saying: "Muhammad (ﷺ) will intercede for us." So Allah the Exalted made clear that his intercession would not benefit the disbelievers of Mecca even if they were his relatives, just as the intercession of Noah for his wife and the intercession of Lot for his wife would not benefit them, despite their closeness to them, because of their disbelief. It was said to them: "Enter the Fire along with those who enter," in the Hereafter, just as it is said to the disbelievers of Mecca and others. Then it was said: Noah's wife may be a substitute for "a parable" under the assumption of an omitted modifier, meaning: Allah struck a parable, the likeness of Noah's wife. And it is permissible for both to be objects (two accusatives).

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 66, verse 11:**

God's words: ﴿And God sets forth an example for those who believe: the wife of Pharaoh﴾. Her name was Asiya bint Muzahim.

Yahya ibn Sallam said: God's words "God sets forth an example for those who disbelieve" are an example God struck to warn Aisha and Hafsa against opposing and conspiring against the Messenger of God (ﷺ) when the two of them banded together against him. Then He set forth for them the examples of the wife of Pharaoh and Maryam bint Imran, to encourage them to hold fast to obedience and to remain steadfast in the religion.

It was also said: this is an exhortation to the believers to be patient in hardship, meaning: do not be weaker in patience under hardship than the wife of Pharaoh, who endured the harm of Pharaoh. Asiya had believed in Musa. It was also said that she was the paternal aunt of Musa, who believed in him. Abu al-Aliyah said: Pharaoh discovered that his wife had come to faith. He came out before the chiefs and said to them: "What do you know about Asiya bint Muzahim?" They praised her. He said to them: "She worships a lord other than me." They said to him: "Kill her." So he drove stakes for her, bound her hands and feet, and she said: ﴿My Lord, build for me a house with You in the Garden﴾. This coincided with Pharaoh's presence, and she laughed when she saw her house in the Garden. Pharaoh said: "Do you not marvel at her madness? We torment her and she laughs!" Then her soul was taken.

Salman al-Farisi, in what Uthman al-Nahdi related from him, said: she was tormented by the sun. When the heat of the sun harmed her, the angels shaded her with their wings.

It was also said: he nailed her hands and feet in the sun and placed a millstone on her back, but God let her see her place in the Garden, until she saw her place in Paradise.

It was also said: when she said, ﴿My Lord, build for me a house with You in the Garden﴾, she was shown her house in the Garden being built. It was also said that it was made of a pearl, related from al-Hasan.

When she said, ﴿And save me﴾, God saved her with the most honorable salvation and raised her to the Garden, where she eats, drinks and enjoys herself.

The meaning of ﴿from Pharaoh and his deeds﴾: by "deeds" she meant disbelief. It was also said: "from his deeds" means from his punishment, his injustice and his gloating. Ibn Abbas said: it means sexual intercourse.

﴿And save me from the wrongdoing people﴾.

Al-Kalbi said: they are the people of Egypt. Muqatil said: they are the Copts. Al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan said: God saved her with the most honorable salvation, raised her to the Garden, and there she eats and drinks.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 66, verse 12:

Allah's words, ﴿And Maryam, daughter of ʿImran﴾: that is, remember Maryam. It has also been said that it is coordinated with (ma'tuf ʿala) "the wife of Pharaoh." The meaning is: Allah set forth as a parable Maryam bint ʿImran and her patience under the harm of the Jews.

﴿Who guarded her chastity﴾: that is, from immoral acts. The exegetes said: by "her chastity" (farj) here He meant the opening of her garment at the collar (jayb), because He said: ﴿So We breathed into it of Our Spirit﴾, and Jibril (peace be upon him) only blew into her collar and did not blow into her private part. In the recitation of Ubayy it reads: "So We breathed into her collar of Our Spirit." Every tear in a garment is called a jayb, and from this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And there are no rifts in it?﴾ [Qaf: 6] [See vol. 17, p. 6.] It is possible that she guarded her chastity and the Spirit was breathed into her collar. The meaning of ﴿So We breathed﴾ is: We sent Jibril, and he blew into her collar of Our Spirit, that is, a spirit from Our spirits, and it was the spirit of ʿIsa. Its explanation has already passed in full at the end of surah al-Nisa', and praise be to Allah. [See vol. 6, p. (22).]

﴿And she affirmed the words of her Lord﴾: the common recitation is "wa-saddaqat" with the doubled letter (tashdid). Hamid and al-Umawi recited "wa-sadaqat" without the doubling (takhfif). ﴿The words of her Lord﴾ refers to Jibril's saying to her: "I am only a messenger of your Lord," [Maryam: 19] and the verse. Muqatil said: by "the words" is meant ʿIsa, and that he is a prophet, and ʿIsa is a word of Allah. This has already been mentioned. [See vol. 4, p. (83).] Al-Hasan and Abu al-ʿAliyah recited "bi-kalimati rabbiha wa-kitabihi" (with "the word of her Lord and His book"). Abu ʿAmr and Hafs, from ʿAsim, recited "wa-kutubihi" in the plural. From Abu Raja' [it is narrated as] "wa-kutubihi" with the taʾ lightened. The rest recited "bi-kitabihi" in the singular. "The Book" is intended as a genus, so it carries the meaning of every book Allah, Exalted is He, has sent down.

﴿And she was among the obedient (al-qanitin)﴾: that is, among the obedient. It has also been said: among those who prayed between Maghrib and ʿIsha'. The reason He did not say "al-qanitat" (feminine plural) is that He intended "she was among the obedient people (al-qawm al-qanitin)." It is also permissible to refer this to the people of her household, for they were obedient to Allah. From Muʿadh ibn Jabal, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Khadijah while she was giving up her soul: "Do you dislike what has befallen you? Allah has placed good in what is disliked. When you arrive before your co-wives [Al-Tabarani narrated from Saʿd ibn Junadah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Allah has married me, in Paradise, to Maryam bint ʿImran, the wife of Pharaoh, and the sister of Musa.'], then convey my greetings to them: Maryam bint ʿImran, Asiyah bint Muzahim, and Kalimah [In b, h, z, s, t, l, h: 'Kalimah'] – or he said Hakimah [In b, h, z, s, t, l, h: 'Halimah'] – bint ʿImran, sister of Musa ibn ʿImran." She said: "With blessing and children, O Messenger of Allah." And Qatadah narrated from Anas, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Four are sufficient for you among the women of the worlds: Maryam bint ʿImran, Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, Fatimah bint Muhammad, and Asiyah the wife of Pharaoh, daughter of Muzahim." The discussion of this has already passed in full under ʿImran, and praise be to Allah.
